notes.1: Many candidates scored full marks on this question. Direction of motion is 28.0° above the horizontal
notes.2: This question was well done. An energy equation was usually set up which resulted in a quadratic equation. Extension at the lowest point is 0.263m.
notes.3i: Candidates often managed to find the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity at the point when the ball hit the ground. The speed was then calculated by using Pythagoras’s theorem. The angle of direction was then found by using trigonometry.
notes.3iii: Many candidates found the required distance. Answers: (i) Speed = 5 ms–1, Angle above the horizontal = 78.5°
notes.4i: By resolving vertically the tension was found. Some candidates made errors in calculating the angle needed to find the vertical component of the tension.

notes.6: This proved to be a difficult question.
notes.6i: A moment equation about the base of F was needed.
notes.6b: A moment equation involving toppling has to be set up. This equation is 4(1.2 – 0.4) ≺ 16(1.2 – 0.4)tan θ
notes.6biii: A diagram with F sitting on its curved surface would help to find the correct distances needed. Trigonometry is then used to find the required angle. Answers: (i) Distance of the centre of mass of F from its larger plane face = 0.174m
notes.7: This was a difficult question for many candidates.
notes.7i: In order to start this part of the question it was necessary to set up an equation using Newton’s Second Law. This equation should be 0.2a = 0.2vdv/dx = –k/(1 – x). The variables must now be separated and then an integration applied. Using the correct limits will give the value of k.
notes.7iii: Another equation is formed by using Newton’s Second Law. The variables can be be separated and integration applied. From this result the value of v can be found. Answers: (i) k = 0.1803
